title: Chapter 8 — The Americans Combat Individualism By The Principle Of Interest Rightly Understood
paragraphs: When the world was managed by a few rich and powerful individuals, these people liked to hold a lofty idea of the duties of man. They were fond of declaring that it is praiseworthy to forget oneself, and that good should be done without hope of reward, as God himself does it. Such were the standard moral opinions of that time. I doubt whether men were more virtuous in aristocratic ages than in others. But they talked ceaselessly about the beauty of virtue, and they studied its usefulness only in private. But now that the imagination takes less lofty flights and every man’s thoughts are centered on himself, moralists are alarmed by this idea of self-sacrifice, and they no longer dare to offer it to the human mind. They therefore content themselves with asking whether the personal advantage of each member of the community does not lie in working for the good of all. When they hit on some point where private interest and public interest meet and merge, they are eager to bring it to notice. Observations of this kind gradually multiply. What was only a single remark becomes a general principle, and it is held to be true that man serves himself in serving his fellow creatures, and that his private interest is to do good.

I have already shown, in several parts of this work, by what means the inhabitants of the United States almost always manage to combine their own advantage with that of their fellow citizens. My purpose now is to point out the general rule that enables them to do so. In the United States hardly anybody talks of the beauty of virtue, but they maintain that virtue is useful, and they prove it every day. American moralists do not claim that men ought to sacrifice themselves for their fellow creatures because it is noble to make such sacrifices. They boldly declare that such sacrifices are as necessary to the person who makes them as to the person for whose sake they are made. They have found that in their country and their age man is driven back upon himself by an irresistible force. They have lost all hope of stopping that force, so they turn all their thought to directing it. They therefore do not deny that every man may follow his own interest, but they try to prove that it is in the interest of every man to be virtuous. I shall not go into the reasons they give here, which would take me away from my subject. It is enough to say that they have convinced their fellow countrymen.

Montaigne said long ago: “Were I not to follow the straight road for its straightness, I should follow it for having found by experience that in the end it is commonly the happiest and most useful track.” The doctrine of self-interest properly understood is therefore not new. But among the Americans of our time it is universally accepted. It has become popular there. You can trace it at the bottom of all their actions, and you will notice it in everything they say. It is as often heard on the lips of the poor man as of the rich. In Europe the principle of interest is much cruder than it is in America, but at the same time it is less common, and above all it is less openly avowed. Among us, men still constantly pretend to a great self-denial that they no longer feel. The Americans, on the contrary, are fond of explaining almost every action of their lives by the principle of self-interest properly understood. They show with satisfaction how an enlightened regard for themselves constantly prompts them to help each other, and inclines them to sacrifice willingly a portion of their time and property to the welfare of the state. In this respect I think they often fail to do themselves justice. In the United States, as elsewhere, people are sometimes seen to yield to the disinterested and spontaneous impulses that are natural to man. But the Americans seldom admit that they give way to emotions of this kind. They are more anxious to do honor to their philosophy than to themselves.

I might stop here, without trying to pass judgment on what I have described. The extreme difficulty of the subject would be my excuse, but I shall not use it. I would rather have my readers, once they see my aim clearly, refuse to follow me than leave them in suspense. The principle of self-interest properly understood is not a lofty one, but it is clear and sure. It does not aim at mighty objects, but it reaches, without excessive effort, all those at which it does aim. Since it lies within the reach of all minds, everyone can grasp and remember it without difficulty. It fits human weaknesses admirably, and so it easily gains great dominion. Nor is that dominion precarious, since the principle checks one personal interest with another and uses, to direct the passions, the very same instrument that excites them. The principle of self-interest properly understood produces no great acts of self-sacrifice, but it suggests small acts of self-denial every day. By itself it cannot make a man virtuous. But it trains a number of citizens in habits of regularity, temperance, moderation, foresight, and self-command. If it does not lead men straight to virtue by the will, it gradually draws them in that direction by their habits. If the principle of self-interest properly understood were to sway the whole moral world, extraordinary virtues would doubtless be rarer. But I think gross depravity would then be less common too. The principle perhaps keeps some men from rising far above the level of mankind. But a great number of other men, who were falling far below it, are caught and held back by it. Look at a few individuals, and they are lowered by it. Look at mankind as a whole, and it is raised. I am not afraid to say that the principle of self-interest properly understood seems to me the best suited of all philosophical theories to the needs of the men of our time, and that I regard it as their chief remaining protection against themselves. The minds of the moralists of our age should therefore turn toward it. Even if they judge it incomplete, they must still adopt it as necessary.

On the whole I do not think there is more egotism among us than in America. The only difference is that there it is enlightened and here it is not. Every American will sacrifice a portion of his private interests to preserve the rest. We would like to preserve the whole, and often the whole is lost. Everybody I see around me seems bent on teaching his contemporaries, by precept and example, that what is useful is never wrong. Will nobody undertake to make them understand how what is right may be useful? No power on earth can prevent the growing equality of conditions from inclining the human mind to seek out what is useful, or from leading every member of the community to be wrapped up in himself. We must therefore expect that personal interest will become more than ever the principal, if not the sole, spring of men’s actions. But it remains to be seen how each man will understand his personal interest. Suppose the members of a community, as they become more equal, also become more ignorant and coarse. Then it is hard to foresee to what pitch of stupid excess their egotism may lead them, and no one can foretell into what disgrace and wretchedness they would plunge themselves rather than sacrifice something of their own well-being to the prosperity of their fellow creatures. I do not think that the system of interest, as it is professed in America, is self-evident in all its parts. But it contains a great number of truths so evident that men, if only they are educated, cannot fail to see them. Educate them, then, at any rate. The age of unquestioning self-sacrifice and instinctive virtues is already drifting far away from us, and the time is fast approaching when freedom, public peace, and social order itself will not be able to exist without education.
